title: Yusuf is ready to go
body: Yusuf has packed for the road. He says linen sells for more in Damascus, where the weavers want good plain cloth. He asks to take ten loads of your linen. The caravan, the group of travellers he will join, charges a fee for a place in the line.

choices.label: Send Yusuf with ten loads of linen
choices.hint: Damascus may pay more than Cairo does.

choices.label: Not this season
choices.hint: Nothing now. Yusuf will be disappointed.

note: Cairo's merchants sent goods by river, desert road and sea. They had long used agents to buy and sell for them in other towns.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 41 to 59 and p. 80 n. 48; Cairo, the Nile boats and the caravan to Damascus
the Geniza letters, mostly 950 to 1250: agents writing home

title: A neighbour wants your linen
body: Abu Bakr makes sails and needs cloth today. He offers a little over Cairo's price for ten loads of your linen, 455 dinars in coin at once.

choices.label: Sell them now
choices.hint: You get 455 dinars today, 5 more than Cairo pays. The linen leaves your warehouse.

choices.label: Keep them for the next trip
choices.hint: Nothing now. The linen stays yours, in the warehouse or on your own trips. In three seasons Abu Bakr thinks the better of a merchant who plans ahead.

choices.label: Say no, and thank him
choices.hint: He will think well of a polite answer.

note: Egyptian linen was woven for export. Ports across the Mediterranean paid more for it than Cairo did, though how much more is a guess.

sources.at: the direction of the price gap only
the direction of the price gap only

title: One load of silk by spring
body: Nabil is a broker, a go-between who finds buyers. He knows a rich family that wants one load of silk before spring. They will pay well, but silk is hard to find.

choices.label: Send to Damascus for the silk
choices.hint: The silk is a venture, so it costs a lot. The family may come back.

choices.label: Say no politely
choices.hint: Nabil trusts you a little less.

note: In 1326 the sultan owned a silk funduq in Alexandria. A funduq was a warehouse and inn for merchants.

sources.at: the property list of 16 April 1326
Background n. 17; qaysariyya, funduq, khan and wikala as one type of building

title: Amina needs money for fuel
body: Amina runs a sugar refinery in Fustat. She needs money now for fuel and cane. She will sell you three loads of sugar for 140 dinars if you pay today.

choices.label: Buy three loads of her sugar
choices.hint: Sugar keeps well, and three loads is a venture, so the sum is large.

choices.label: Wish her luck and pass
choices.hint: You keep your money. Amina will find another buyer, and she will not forget it.

note: In about 1400 a writer in Cairo counted 65 places that refined sugar in Fustat. Thirteen belonged to merchants.

sources.at: p. 149; the count of Ibn Duqmaq, who died in 1406

title: Share a funduq
body: Khalid is one of the Karimi, a loose group of great spice merchants. He and his friends are building a funduq, a warehouse and inn for merchants, in a port on the spice road. He offers your house a share of the rooms for one trip.

choices.label: Take a share of the rooms
choices.hint: You share the costs, and the news.

choices.label: Keep your own lodging
choices.hint: You pay no share, and you hear less. Partners like a steady house.

note: The Karimi were a loose group of spice merchants. Now and then they built funduqs together, for shared use.

sources.at: pp. 149 and 150; the loose confederation and the funduqs built for common purposes

title: Salih will buy the linen
body: Salih is a broker, a go-between who finds goods and buyers. He knows a grower with six loads of linen to sell. He offers to buy all of it for your house while you stay at your desk.

choices.label: Let Salih buy it alone
choices.hint: It is quick, but some bales may be poor. Salih keeps a bigger share, so the six loads cost 215 dinars.

choices.label: Have him bring every bale to your desk
choices.hint: You look at each one before you pay. It costs a day, and you get good linen.

choices.label: Not this time
choices.hint: Salih will look for another buyer.

note: A Geniza letter asked a merchant in a flax town to watch a broker. Flax is the plant that linen is made from. He was not to let the broker buy middling flax for the writer. He was also not to pay the broker in debased coins, so the broker would not turn against the writer.

sources.at: pp. 278 to 279; the broker, the middling flax and the debased dinars

title: Rizq has a job for Yusuf
body: Rizq is a draper, a cloth seller. He asks Yusuf to take a bundle of fine cloth to {to} and sell it. For this special job he will pay a fee of 7 dinars. He pays it to the house, but the job is Yusuf's.

choices.label: Pass the fee on to Yusuf
choices.hint: You gain nothing. Yusuf gets all of it and trusts you more.

choices.label: Split the fee with Yusuf
choices.hint: You gain 4 dinars now. Yusuf is content.

choices.label: Keep the whole fee for the house
choices.hint: You gain 7 dinars. Yusuf will know.

note: In the Geniza papers an agent who did a special job was paid a commission, a fee for that job alone. It did not pay for the friendship.

sources.at: p. 316; the commission paid for a special service, not for the relationship

title: Wadud wants linen for the east
body: Wadud sells cloth to merchants who ship it far to the east. He has heard that your house keeps its word. He asks for four loads of linen from your warehouse. He offers 200 dinars, or he will take two loads now and ask for more later.

choices.label: Sell him four loads
choices.hint: He pays at once. He will tell others.

choices.label: Sell him two loads
choices.hint: You keep the rest of your linen. He comes back for more and pays 20 more.

choices.label: Keep the linen for your own trips
choices.hint: Wadud buys from someone else. All your linen stays in your warehouse for your own trips. You earn nothing now. In three seasons dealers say your house plans ahead.

note: A historian of Mamluk cloth writes that cloth and metalwork were the largest Mamluk exports to the Far East. This was from the 1200s to the 1400s. She takes it from two earlier writers. She does not say which cloths.

sources.at: p. 168, citing Mackie 1984 and Bloom 1999; Mamluk fabrics and metalwork among the largest exports to the Far East

title: Samir is home from {to}
body: Samir is home from {to} after {seasons}. He asks to go out again, and he asks for a qirad.

choices.label: Send him again under a qirad
choices.hint: He keeps a third. The next sheet shows the cost.

choices.label: Give him a bonus of 5 dinars first
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars, and the trip must have made at least that much. He will be loyal.

choices.label: Let him rest a season
choices.hint: He is glad of it. He can go out later.

note: In the contracts Goitein read, the traveller's share was normally one third.

sources.at: p. 317; the worker's smaller share, normally one third

title: Yusuf is home with news
body: Yusuf is home from {to}. You told him he could go further if the price was better. He says a merchant from Persia heard of your house on the road and wants to deal with it.

choices.label: Meet the Persian merchant
choices.hint: It costs a gift of 8 dinars. In three seasons the Persian pays you 12.

choices.label: Turn him down
choices.hint: Yusuf is glad of a safe road. Your other agents hear of it in two seasons.

note: The Persian merchant is invented. We found no recorded prices for the road from Damascus to Aleppo, or on to Tabriz. So the game's prices there are guesses.

sources.at: estimate; no recorded prices for the road from Damascus to Aleppo and on to Tabriz were found; the Tabriz passage is vol. 2, pp. 339 to 341

title: Pepper is dear in Damascus
body: Zayd is a broker, a go-between who finds goods and buyers. He says pepper sells for far more in Damascus than in Cairo. It comes up from Aden by the Red Sea. He has two loads to sell you at today's price.

choices.label: Buy two loads of pepper
choices.hint: It costs 250 dinars, a big sum, because pepper for Damascus is a venture. Sending it to Damascus is up to you.

choices.label: Pay Zayd to watch Damascus
choices.hint: It costs 9 dinars. He writes to you when the price moves.

choices.label: Not now
choices.hint: Zayd will find another buyer.

note: The Karimi merchants brought spices from Aden to Cairo, Alexandria and Damascus. A lawsuit of 1097 to 1098 tells of a merchant in Fustat. He had told his agent to hand half the goods to the trustee of the merchants at Aden. The trustee was to buy pepper on the Malabar coast of India.

sources.at: p. 149; the Karimi brought spices from Aden to Cairo, Alexandria and Damascus
no. 36, introduction; the agent told to hand half the goods to the trustee of the merchants at Aden, to buy pepper on the Malabar coast, in a lawsuit of 1097 to 1098

title: Linen sells at Constantinople
body: Bishara is a broker. He says buyers at Constantinople want flax and linen from Egypt. Flax is the plant that linen is made from. He offers to buy three loads of your linen today, at Cairo's price.

choices.label: Sell him three loads
choices.hint: You get 135 dinars now. The road to Constantinople stays free for other goods.

choices.label: Keep the linen for a trip
choices.hint: Constantinople pays about 25 dinars more for three loads, but it is a long way off. Damp spoils one load before you can send them.

choices.label: Ask him to write to Constantinople
choices.hint: It costs 9 dinars. You learn who is buying.

note: Pegolotti wrote a handbook for merchants about 1340. It lists flax of Alexandria among the goods sold at Constantinople and Pera.

sources.at: the section on flax of Alexandria sold at Constantinople and Pera, which names the place and the good; 1766 printing pp. 16 to 17; the 1936 Evans page not confirmed

title: The galleys want pepper
body: Fakhr is a broker in Cairo. He has news from Alexandria. Venice's galleys, long ships with oars, are back, and their buyers want pepper. He has two loads to sell you at today's price.

choices.label: Buy two loads of pepper
choices.hint: It costs 260 dinars, a big sum, because pepper for the galleys is a venture. The galley buyers are at Alexandria.

choices.label: Pay Fakhr to watch the harbour
choices.hint: It costs 9 dinars. He writes when the galleys sail.

choices.label: Not now
choices.hint: Fakhr will find another buyer.

note: Venice sent its state galleys to Alexandria in yearly convoys from 1301. The service stopped after the galleys came home in 1312. A convoy is a group of ships that sail together.

sources.at: p. 117; the galley convoys of 1301 to 1312
p. 137 and note 116; the galley service resumed in 1345

title: Sugar sells in Cyprus
body: Amr is a broker. He says Italian buyers wait at Famagusta, on Cyprus, for sugar from Egypt. Venice's trade with Alexandria is hampered, so they meet our goods there. He has three loads to sell you today.

choices.label: Buy three loads of sugar
choices.hint: It costs 140 dinars, a big sum, because sugar for Cyprus is a venture. Famagusta pays more, but sending it is up to you.

choices.label: Ask him to name the buyers
choices.hint: It costs 9 dinars. You learn who is buying.

choices.label: Not now
choices.hint: Amr will find another buyer.

note: Venice forbade its merchants to trade in Egypt from 1323, and its ships came back in 1345. Famagusta, on Cyprus, was a go-between for Venice and Egypt, as it had been since before the ban.

sources.at: pp. 135 to 136; Famagusta as the market and go-between for Venice and Egypt, a role older than the ban of 1323

title: Silver from the eastern mountains
body: Farrukh makes silver cups in Cairo. He hears that a mountain near Samarkand has a silver mine that is easy to work. He wants to pay for a first lot of silver and asks you to put in some money too.

choices.label: Pay for a lot at the mine
choices.hint: It costs 10 dinars now. In three seasons the silversmiths of Cairo speak well of you.

choices.label: Pay for a small lot
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now. Merchants from the east hear that you trade far away.

choices.label: Wish Farrukh luck and decline
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Farrukh will find another partner.

note: A Persian writer said in 1340 that a mountain near Samarkand has an easy silver mine that pays well. He copied from older books, so this may be older news.

title: Quseir or Aydhab
body: Ghazi ships goods to the Red Sea. He asks if you want them sent by Quseir or by Aydhab. Quseir is the port nearest Qus. But the sea voyage from it is hard, because fierce north winds blow against the ships.

choices.label: Ship by Quseir
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now and 1 more in two seasons, for the slow sail. The desert road is short.

choices.label: Ship by Aydhab
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. The desert road is longer, but the sea is quicker, and partners like that.

choices.label: Split the goods between the two
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. If one road fails, the other still brings goods, and foreign houses notice.

note: Quseir was the port nearest Qus, but ships sailing from it fought fierce north winds. Al-Qalqashandi, who wrote this about 1400, says some merchants chose it anyway.

sources.at: p. 32 (the preference for Quseir is al-Qalqashandi, about 1400)

title: Pepper waits for the ships
body: Salim is a pepper dealer in Aden. He writes that news from Egypt is poor, so pepper will hardly sell until a week before the ships sail. He asks if he should hold your pepper until then.

choices.label: Hold it to the last week
choices.hint: It costs 3 dinars now, for storage. Buyers come from far away at the end, and partners hear of the good price.

choices.label: Sell early
choices.hint: Salim sells 1 lot of pepper for 60 dinars now. The price is low, and partners hear of that too.

note: A merchant's letter from Aden of about 1135 says pepper would not sell until the week before the ships sailed. Then buyers came from afar, and the price was set at 23 dinars a bahar.

sources.at: pp. 342 to 343 (letter II,23, about 1135)

title: Pepper dried in the sun
body: Rahim is a broker in Calicut. It is autumn, and the new pepper lies on mats in the sun until it dries and turns black. He offers you a lot at the harvest price.

choices.label: Buy two lots at harvest
choices.hint: It costs 200 dinars now for 2 lots of pepper, the harvest price with the cost of shipping. The pepper reaches your warehouse in three seasons, and partners think well of you.

choices.label: Buy one lot
choices.hint: It costs 100 dinars now for 1 lot of pepper, with the cost of shipping. It reaches your warehouse in two seasons, and foreign houses see that you buy at the source.

choices.label: Wait for later prices
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Rahim sells to another house.

note: Ibn Battuta wrote that in autumn pepper was gathered and spread on mats in the sun until it dried and turned black. At Calicut he saw it poured out and measured by the bushel, like millet.

title: Where India meets Persia
body: Bilal is a broker in Hormuz, a port on an island. He writes that goods from India are sent on from there to buyers in Persia. He asks if you will send a buyer of your own.

choices.label: Send a buyer to Hormuz
choices.hint: It costs 10 dinars now. The road is long, and foreign houses think well of you.

choices.label: Buy from Aden instead
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. The road is shorter, and partners like it.

choices.label: Wait
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Bilal tells his other friends.

note: New Hormuz, on an island, was founded shortly after 1300. Ibn Battuta wrote that it was the port of India and Sind, whose goods went on to Iraq, Fars and Khurasan.

sources.at: vol. 2, p. 400 and note 118

title: Salt is dearer in Mali
body: Hamdan is a salt dealer in Walata. He says a load of salt sells for far more in Mali than here. He offers to buy some for you at the mine town of Taghaza.

choices.label: Buy two lots of salt
choices.hint: It costs 20 dinars now for 2 lots of salt at Taghaza. The salt reaches your warehouse in three seasons, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Buy one lot
choices.hint: It costs 10 dinars now for 1 lot of salt. It reaches your warehouse in three seasons, and partners think it a careful trade.

choices.label: Wait for another year
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Hamdan sells to another house.

note: In 1352 Ibn Battuta wrote that salt cost eight to ten mithqals a load at Walata, and twenty to thirty in Mali. This is later evidence, after the game's years.

title: What goes south for gold
body: Bakr asks what goods go south across the Sahara, and what comes back. He wants to send a load of goods from your house. He asks what to choose.

choices.label: Send salt and copper
choices.hint: It costs 9 dinars now. The goods cross the Sahara, and foreign houses think well of you.

choices.label: Send cowries
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars now. Cowries are small shells used as money, and partners like a light load.

choices.label: Decline
choices.hint: It costs nothing. Bakr sends his own goods.

note: Al-Umari wrote, from older accounts, that merchants left Sijilmasa for the lands south of the Sahara with salt, copper and cowries. They came back with gold.

sources.at: p. 202 (the Sijilmasa entry)

title: Copper in rods
body: A dealer at Takadda offers copper rods for your goods. The rods are a span and a half long, and a thick rod is worth more than a thin one. He asks if you will take rods or gold.

choices.label: Take rods
choices.hint: It costs 60 dinars now for 2 lots of copper in rods. The rods travel well and reach your warehouse in three seasons, and partners hear of it.

choices.label: Take gold instead
choices.hint: It costs 100 dinars now for 1 chest of gold. Gold is light and reaches your warehouse in two seasons, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Decline
choices.hint: It costs nothing. The dealer trades with another house.

note: In 1353, after the game's years, Ibn Battuta wrote that Takadda's copper was made into rods a span and a half long. Four hundred thick or six or seven hundred thin rods were worth one gold mithqal, and thin ones bought meat and firewood.

title: Room for pepper
body: A Genoese buyer asks you to book space for pepper at Alexandria. Pepper is packed for the ships in a sporta, a big load. He asks how many you will book.

choices.label: Book ten sporte
choices.hint: It costs 12 dinars now. The pepper sells when the ships return, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Book five
choices.hint: It costs 6 dinars now. It is a smaller venture, and partners think it careful.

choices.label: Refuse
choices.hint: It costs nothing. The buyer books with another house.

note: At Alexandria pepper was packed in a big load called a sporta, five cantars in all. Pegolotti reckoned it cost seven gold bezants to ship one to Venice in the armed galleys.

sources.at: Pagnini 1766 printing, pp. 58 and 61

title: Cheap goods in winter
body: Rafiq says there are cheap goods in Alexandria now, because the foreign ships have gone home. Prices will rise when the buyers return in spring.

choices.label: Send a ship in winter
choices.hint: It costs 240 dinars now. That is 220 for 2 lots of pepper at the winter price and 20 for the risk of the sea. The pepper reaches your warehouse in two seasons, and foreign houses admire your nerve.

choices.label: Send a Nile boat to the warehouses
choices.hint: It costs 113 dinars now, 110 for 1 lot of pepper and 3 for the boat. The choice of goods is small, and the pepper reaches your warehouse in two seasons. Partners like the care.

choices.label: Wait for the spring crowd
choices.hint: It costs nothing. You pay the dear price later.

note: In the 1200s a merchant who sailed to Egypt in winter could buy unsold goods cheaply. The foreign merchants had gone home, and the buyers came back in spring.

title: The clearest glass
body: A Persian buyer asks you to find glass bottles of the very clearest kind. He will pay well for them in the east.

choices.label: Order from the glass houses of Aleppo
choices.hint: It costs 100 dinars now for 2 lots of the clearest glass. The glass reaches your warehouse in two seasons, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Order from Alexandria
choices.hint: It costs 70 dinars now for 2 lots of plainer glass. It is cheaper and less clear, and partners like the price. It reaches your warehouse in two seasons.

choices.label: Decline
choices.hint: It costs nothing. The buyer asks another house.

note: In 1340 the Persian writer Mustawfi wrote that the best glass makers were those of Aleppo.

title: Red dye from an insect
body: A dyer asks you for a crimson dye that comes from an insect gathered on the plains near Tabriz. He will pay well for it.

choices.label: Order a lot
choices.hint: It costs 10 dinars now, your share of the order. The dye sells dear, and foreign houses hear of it.

choices.label: Order a small lot
choices.hint: It costs 4 dinars now. It is a small venture, and partners like it.

choices.label: Decline
choices.hint: It costs nothing. The dyer asks another house.

note: In 1340 Mustawfi wrote that the crimson dye kermes could be gathered south of Marand in one week of summer. After that the insect flew away.
